result: The study employed 49 healthy English speakers who completed 200 choice trials across four set sizes (9, 16, 25, 36 items), with eye tracking, choice, and response time data collected. Post-choice, subjects rated each food item on a -3 to 3 scale, which served as the measure of item value.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 and C67-C79 provide comprehensive methodological details about the experimental design, participant characteristics, data collection procedures, and ethical approvals. The experimental setup is well-documented with appropriate sample size justification, clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, and detailed eye tracking methodology including multiple calibrations and quality control measures.

result: Visual attention patterns showed that the probability and duration of gazes to items increased with item rating and decreased with set size. Initial gazes were shorter than returning gazes, and last gazes to chosen items were longer than to non-chosen items.
evaluation: Claims C7-C14 report consistent statistical findings with appropriate mixed-effects regression analyses, including effect sizes and 94% HDI intervals. The patterns are internally consistent and align with the visual data presented in Figure 2. The statistical approach appropriately accounts for within-subject variability.

result: Visual search trajectories revealed systematic patterns: subjects started at screen center, moved to the top-left corner, then searched top-to-bottom while increasingly focusing on highly-rated and larger items. Return gaze probability and duration increased over trial time.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 describe visual search patterns supported by time-binned regression analyses shown in Figure 3. The methodology appropriately normalizes time and uses mixed-effects models to track how item attributes influence gaze over the course of trials. The findings are well-supported by both statistical analyses and visual representations.

result: Cumulative gaze time was influenced by item rating, size, position, and set size, but actual choice probability depended only on item rating and set size, not on item size or position.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23 demonstrate an important dissociation between what drives visual attention versus what drives choice. The statistical analyses appropriately test multiple predictors and show that while physical attributes (size, position) influence gaze allocation, they do not influence final choice, suggesting value-based rather than salience-based choice mechanisms.

result: Subjects chose the highest-rated seen item 84% of the time but did not look at all items (fraction decreased with set size), and response times increased with set size. This pattern ruled out strict optimal choice models requiring complete search.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 provide critical evidence against optimal choice models through multiple converging measures. The finding that subjects don't examine all items yet maintain high accuracy for seen items is well-documented with appropriate statistics. The inference in C28 logically follows from the empirical observations.

result: Subjects chose the last-seen item only about 44% of the time, clearly rejecting the hard satisficing model which predicts choice of the last-seen item.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C102 provide direct evidence against hard satisficing through a simple but powerful test. The ~44% rate is substantially below what would be expected if subjects stopped searching immediately upon finding an acceptable item. The statistical analysis appropriately examines this across set sizes and trial types.

result: Stopping probability increased with both cached value and elapsed time, while decreasing with set size, consistent with probabilistic satisficing.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32 provide evidence supporting probabilistic satisficing models. The statistical analysis appropriately tests the key predictions of the model with clear effect sizes and confidence intervals. However, the authors note this finding alone cannot discriminate between probabilistic satisficing and evidence accumulation models.

result: All subjects showed positive gaze influence on choice (ranging 1.7-75%), which increased with set size. Choice probability increased with cumulative gaze advantage, and subjects with stronger gaze influence were less likely to choose the highest-rated item but more likely to choose the last-seen item.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 document the gaze-choice relationship using an appropriate residual-based measure that controls for item values. The findings are internally consistent and align with predictions from gaze-driven evidence accumulation models. The negative correlation between gaze influence and optimal choice accuracy (C36) is particularly important for model discrimination.

result: Subjects with stronger rating influence on gaze allocation looked at fewer items, were more likely to choose the highest-rated seen item, and more likely to choose the last-seen item.
evaluation: Claim C39 describes important individual differences in search strategy. The statistical analyses appropriately characterize how rating-driven attention relates to choice behavior. These findings suggest that value-guided attention leads to more efficient search and better outcomes.

result: Model comparison using WAIC showed that active-gaze models consistently outperformed passive-gaze models (82-94% of subjects across set sizes). The PSM+ won the plurality of comparisons in each set size, though PSM+ and GLAM+ were not meaningfully different from each other.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 and C54 report comprehensive model comparison results using appropriate information criteria (WAIC). The statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni correction) are appropriate for comparing model distributions. The finding that active-gaze models consistently outperform passive-gaze models is robust across set sizes.

result: Model validation showed PSM+ and GLAM+ accurately recovered mean RT, while IAM+ showed systematic bias (underestimating short, overestimating long RTs). All models underestimated high probabilities of choosing the highest-rated item, with PSM+ providing the most accurate account.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 report appropriate out-of-sample validation using simulation-based posterior predictive checks. The regression analyses comparing predicted to observed values provide clear evidence of model performance. The systematic bias in IAM+ RT predictions is particularly informative for model discrimination.

result: For gaze-choice associations, PSM+ and IAM+ overestimated weak associations while underestimating strong ones, whereas GLAM+ provided the best account, only slightly underestimating strong associations. GLAM+ provided the best overall account when considering the gaze-choice relationship.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C53, and C57 demonstrate that while PSM+ fits choice and RT data slightly better, GLAM+ provides superior account of the gaze-choice relationship. The validation approach appropriately tests model predictions against data not explicitly used in the likelihood-based model comparison. This represents a critical discriminating test between models.

result: PSM+ and GLAM+ showed evidence for both multiplicative and additive gaze biases, with negative correlation between the two (stronger additive bias associated with stronger multiplicative bias). IAM+ showed no evidence for additive gaze bias.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 characterize the gaze bias mechanisms with appropriate parameter estimates and correlational analyses. The finding that IAM+ cannot capture additive gaze biases while also providing poor fit to gaze-choice associations is internally consistent. The negative correlation between γ and ζ in PSM+ and GLAM+ suggests these mechanisms may serve complementary roles.

result: The study concludes that behavior cannot be explained by optimal choice or standard satisficing, but after incorporating active gaze effects, probabilistic satisficing slightly outperforms evidence accumulation models for choice and RT data.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C56, C100-C101 summarize the main findings appropriately. The conclusions are well-supported by the qualitative tests (subjects don't look at all items, don't always choose best seen item) and quantitative model comparisons. However, the superiority of PSM+ is modest and not consistent across all validation metrics.

result: The study demonstrates that gaze actively increases subjective value of attended alternatives rather than passively filtering consideration sets, with choices strongly dependent on actual gaze duration.
evaluation: Claims C55, C103, C105-C106, and C114 articulate the key theoretical contribution. The evidence from active vs. passive model comparisons, combined with the gaze-choice associations, strongly supports this conclusion. This challenges passive attention models common in economics and demonstrates the importance of gaze-weighted value models.

result: The manuscript reviews prior work showing gaze-driven evidence accumulation in binary choice, satisficing in many-alternative choice, and identifies a gap regarding whether gaze-driven frameworks can account for truly large choice sets.
evaluation: Claims C58-C66 and C113 appropriately cite and characterize prior literature. The citations appear relevant and the characterization of the literature gap is reasonable. However, the accuracy of these literature claims cannot be fully verified without checking the cited sources.

result: The study contrasts binary and multi-alternative choice, arguing that in binary choice attending to either alternative is equally useful, whereas with many alternatives it's beneficial to quickly identify and focus on the best items, with choices more driven by gaze in later decision stages.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 provide theoretical interpretation of the differences between binary and multi-alternative choice. The reasoning is logical and supported by the finding that only ratings (not positions/sizes) predict choice. However, C93 makes an implicit claim about binary choice that relies on cited work rather than data from this study.

result: The authors speculate that with aversive foods or reversed framing, gaze effects might be opposite, and that additive and multiplicative biases may have opposite effects in such cases, suggesting need for future research.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are explicitly speculative and identify limitations and future directions. While C98 cites supporting evidence, the speculation in C97 is not directly tested in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not empirically supported by the current data.

result: The authors speculate that PSM+ may perform well due to item repetition allowing learned search, and that model performance may differ in novel vs. familiar environments, suggesting need for future research.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 acknowledge a potential confound in the experimental design (item repetition) and speculate about generalizability. This is appropriate scientific caution, but the speculation is not empirically tested. The examples (vending machines, restaurants) are illustrative but not evidence-based.

result: The computational modeling employed Bayesian parameter estimation using PyMC3 with MCMC sampling, appropriate priors, convergence checks, and model simulations. All analyses were performed in Python with specified software versions, and data/code are publicly available.
evaluation: Claims C80-C92 document the computational methods comprehensively. The Bayesian approach with MCMC is appropriate, convergence diagnostics are specified, and the inclusion of spurious trials (5%) follows established practice. The public availability of data and code (C92) supports reproducibility. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

result: The authors conclude that findings provide new insight into search and choice mechanisms and demonstrate the importance of process-tracing techniques and computational modeling for decision-making research.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108 state appropriate broader implications. The study does demonstrate the value of combining eye tracking with computational modeling, and the findings do advance understanding of many-alternative choice. These are reasonable conclusions supported by the comprehensive empirical and modeling work.

result: The abstract claims that gaze-driven probabilistic satisficing provides slightly better fits to choices and RTs, while gaze-driven evidence accumulation provides the best overall account considering the gaze-choice relationship.
evaluation: Claims C115-C116 accurately summarize the main findings reported in the results section. This nuanced conclusion appropriately reflects that different models excel at different aspects of the data, with PSM+ better for choice/RT and GLAM+ better for gaze-choice associations.
